title: Prediction and Factors Interpretation of Wildfire Susceptibility in Southern California Incorporating Remote Sensing Data into Machine Learning Approaches
content: Accurate wildfire susceptibility prediction in Southern California is vital for regional hazard mitigation and emergency management. Despite the current availability of machine learning (ML) models for predicting wildfire susceptibility, there is a lack of high-performance modeling and interpretation over large amounts of historical fire data for this region. This study evaluates seven ML algorithms—Support Vector Classification (SVC), Logistic Regression (LR), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM)—using 18 geo-environmental and anthropogenic contributing factors in Riverside County from 2012 to 2023. Using a standard random train-test split, the top-performing LGBM model achieved an AUC of 0.97, an accuracy of 91.65%, and an F1-score of 91.51%. However, spatial evaluation via success and prediction rate curves revealed a more conservative and realistic generalizability (AUC = 0.748 and 0.740, respectively), underscoring the localized, non-portable nature of the regional predictors. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) indicated that multi-year rainfall norms, solar radiation, distance to urban centers, and elevation were the primary drivers of model output. This framework provides a benchmark for regional susceptibility mapping while highlighting the essential constraints of spatial validation in fire engineering applications.
